title: Restriction of weak Cartesian structures to the unary fiber
statement:
Use infinity categories, mapping spaces and universes of [def-coef-complete-algebroid] and symmetric monoidal infinity categories of [lem-coef-symmetric-monoidal-segal-classification]. Let $p:\mathcal C^\otimes\to N(\mathsf{Fin}_*)$ be a symmetric monoidal infinity category, with underlying category $\mathcal C=p^{-1}(\langle1\rangle)$. Suppose its unit $\mathbf1$ is terminal and, for every $c,c'$, the canonical maps $c\otimes c'\to c\otimes\mathbf1\simeq c$ and $c\otimes c'\to\mathbf1\otimes c'\simeq c'$ induced by the terminal maps are a product cone. Let $\mathcal D$ be an infinity category with finite products, including a terminal object. A product cone means that its apex $z$ and legs to $d_i$ induce $\operatorname{Map}(t,z)\simeq\prod_i\operatorname{Map}(t,d_i)$ for every $t$; the empty cone means terminality.

Define $W(\mathcal C^\otimes,\mathcal D)$ to be the full infinity subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^\otimes,\mathcal D)$ whose objects are functors $F$ satisfying both conditions: (i) for every $x$ over $\langle n\rangle$, the maps $F(x)\to F(x_i)$ from cocartesian inert projections $x\to x_i$ over $\rho_i$ form a product cone, including $F(x)$ terminal when $n=0$; (ii) $F$ takes every $p$-cocartesian edge over the fold $\mu_n:\langle n\rangle\to\langle1\rangle$ to an equivalence, where $\mu_n(i)=1$ for every non-basepoint, including $n=0$. These functors are called weak Cartesian structures. Let $\operatorname{Fun}^{\mathrm{fp}}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)$ be the full subcategory of functors preserving all finite product cones, including terminal objects. Restriction to the unary fiber is an equivalence of infinity categories
$$W(\mathcal C^\otimes,\mathcal D)\xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }\operatorname{Fun}^{\mathrm{fp}}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D).$$
The assertion includes arbitrary natural transformations and all higher simplices, with no invertibility requirement on a transformation.

source.place: Definition 2.4.0.1, Definition 2.4.1.1 and Proposition 2.4.1.6, printed pp. 282-285; proof on printed pp. 287-290. Online source read; archive WANTED. No Stacks tag states this quasicategorical restriction theorem.

proof.text: First record consequences of the defining conditions on a weak Cartesian structure $H$. It inverts every cocartesian edge $u$ over an active map $\langle n\rangle\to\langle m\rangle$: follow $u$ by a cocartesian fold to the unary fiber. The composite is cocartesian over $\mu_n$, so both that composite and the second edge are inverted; cancellation gives the claim. This includes active unit insertions and the empty tuple. In particular, $H(\mathbf1)$ is terminal, since the nullary fold identifies it with the terminal value of $H$ on the empty tuple. The unit and binary-tensor hypotheses on $C$ also give every finite tensor its canonical product cone, by induction: on mapping spaces each new binary tensor adds one product factor, and the base case is the terminal unit.

Restriction $h=H|_C$ preserves binary products with their actual legs. For $x=(c,d)$ let $s:x\to c\otimes d$ be a cocartesian fold. To check the first leg, put $z=(c,\mathbf1)$, let $e:x\to z$ be $(1_c,d\to\mathbf1)$ in the binary fiber, and let $v:c\to z$ be the cocartesian active inclusion inserting the unit. The inert projection $r:z\to c$ and fold followed by the unitor $q:z\to c$ both compose with $v$ to the identity. Step 1 inverts $v$, hence $H(r)\simeq H(q)$. The composite $re$ is the first inert leg of $x$, whereas $qe$ is $s$ followed by the canonical tensor projection $c\otimes d\to c$. Thus $h$ takes that projection to the first leg of the product cone $H(x)$ after the equivalence $H(s)$. Interchanging the two coordinates proves the other leg. Step 1 gives preservation of the terminal object. Iterating the mapping-space characterization of a binary product now proves preservation of every finite product cone, including any cone equivalent to these chosen ones.

Work in one enlarged universe in which the total operad, cylinder and all comma shapes are small. Use the cylinder $X$ and its full endpoint subcategories $A,B$ from [lem-coef-terminal-unit-active-comma]. Its unary level-zero fiber is the full subcategory $C\subset A$. Define $E\subset\operatorname{Fun}(X,D)$ by requiring all vertical identity-base edges $\gamma_x:(x,0)\to(x,1)$ to be inverted and the level-one restriction to belong to $W$. Define $E_0\subset\operatorname{Fun}(A,D)$ by requiring unary restriction to preserve finite products and every cocartesian active edge to be inverted. Naturality along the vertical edges and steps 1-2 show that restriction $E\to\operatorname{Fun}(A,D)$ lands in $E_0$. All these are full subcategories, so their morphisms remain arbitrary coherent transformations.

Restriction $r:E\to W$ is an equivalence. In fact, for every $(x,0)$, the comma category of arrows from $(x,0)$ into $B$ has initial object $\gamma_x$: its mapping space into an arrow $(x,0)\to(y,1)$ is contractible because the space of arrows $x\to y$ is the same at level one and across the cylinder, and the required triangle is a factorization through the identity. At a level-one object the corresponding comma has its identity as initial object. Apply [lem-coef-relative-limit-initial-components] with one component and the map $D\to *$: a cone on either comma is limiting exactly when its leg at that initial object is an equivalence. Consequently right Kan extension from $B$ is equivalent to inverting the vertical edges. The pointwise right Kan restriction theorem then gives a trivial Kan fibration onto all $\operatorname{Fun}(B,D)$; restrict it over the full subcategory $W$. A section $s:W\to E$ is precomposition with the projection $X\to C^\otimes$.

For $x\in A$ over $\langle n\rangle$, the comma category of arrows from $x$ to $C$ is the lift category of the single active base map $\mu_n:\langle n\rangle\to\langle1\rangle$. A cocartesian fold $s_x:x\to t_x$ is initial there by [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-composition-initiality]. The one-component case of [lem-coef-relative-limit-initial-components] therefore says that $f:A\to D$ is a right Kan extension from $C$ exactly when every $f(s_x)$ is an equivalence. This is equivalent to inverting all cocartesian active edges: one direction includes folds, and the other follows by composing any active edge with a fold as in step 1. Every functor on $C$ admits these pointwise extensions, since the required limits are evaluations at initial objects. Apply the right Kan restriction theorem and restrict over the finite-product-preserving functors. Thus $E_0\to\operatorname{Fun}^{\mathrm{fp}}(C,D)$ is an equivalence of full infinity categories.

Fix $f\in E_0$. The comma category from $A$ to $(x,1)$ has the terminal object $\alpha_x:(x^+,0)\to(x,1)$ by [lem-coef-terminal-unit-active-comma]. Thus every required pointwise colimit is evaluation at $x^+$ by [lem-coef-infinity-final-index-colimit]. Apply the right Kan restriction theorem to opposite categories (with target $D^{\mathrm{op}}$ and base $*$). It supplies left Kan extensions of $f$ along $A\subset X$, and restriction from the full subcategory $L\subset\operatorname{Fun}(X,D)$ of these extensions, with level-zero restriction in $E_0$, is an equivalence $L\to E_0$. By the opposite of the one-component case of [lem-coef-relative-limit-initial-components] (target $D^{\mathrm{op}}\to *$; $\alpha_x$ is initial in the opposite comma), a cocone on this comma is a colimit exactly when its leg at $\alpha_x$ is an equivalence. Hence an extension $F$ lies in $L$ exactly when every $F(\alpha_x)$ is an equivalence. No small colimit completeness of $D$ is used.

We identify $L$ with $E$. Suppose first $F\in L$, with $f=F|_A$. The active inclusion adding an empty output has a cocartesian lift $\beta_x:(x,0)\to(x^+,0)$, since its new coordinate is the tensor unit. Its composite with $\alpha_x$ is the vertical edge $\gamma_x$, up to the unit comparison. Both factors are inverted, the first by $f\in E_0$ and the second by step 6. Hence $F(\gamma_x)$ is an equivalence. For any active cocartesian $u:x\to y$ at level one, the vertical naturality square compares $F(u)$ with $f(u)$ at level zero; its other two edges and $f(u)$ are equivalences. Thus $F(u)$ is an equivalence, giving in particular the fold condition for $F|_B$.

It remains to verify the inert product cones for this $F|_B$. For each inert leg $x\to x_j$, terminality of $\alpha_{x_j}$ in its comma gives a coherent triangle $\alpha_{x_j}\eta_j\simeq(x\to x_j)\alpha_x$ with $\eta_j:x^+\to x_j^+$ in $A$. Concretely its active base map sends $j$ to the retained coordinate and every other input, including the added unit, to the added unit output. The retained component is the identity on $x_j$; the other component is the terminal map to $\mathbf1$. Under the equivalences $f(x^+)\simeq h((\bigotimes_i x_i)\otimes\mathbf1)$ and $f(x_j^+)\simeq h(x_j\otimes\mathbf1)$ induced by folds, $f(\eta_j)$ is $h$ of the canonical projection: folding that active block map tensors the identity on $x_j$ with the terminal maps on the other factors and then applies the unit constraints. These are exactly the defining tensor-product legs. Their source cone is a product by finite iteration of the hypothesis on $C$, and $h=f|_C$ preserves it since $f\in E_0$. The displayed triangles, together with the equivalences $F(\alpha_x)$ and $F(\alpha_{x_j})$, identify this product cone with the required inert cone for $F|_B$. If $n=0$, $x^+=(\mathbf1)$ and $h(\mathbf1)$ is terminal, proving the empty cone as well. Thus $F\in E$.

Conversely let $F\in E$. Factor $\alpha_x$ as the vertical edge at $x^+$ followed by the level-one cocartesian inert projection $\delta_x:x^+\to x$ dropping the added unit. The first factor is inverted by definition of $E$. The product cones for $F|_B$ identify $F(\delta_x)$ with the projection from the product of $F(x)$ and $F(\mathbf1)$ onto $F(x)$: projecting further to each color gives the same inert legs on both sides. Step 1 makes $F(\mathbf1)$ terminal, so this projection is an equivalence by the mapping-space definition of product. This also works for $n=0$, where both the empty product and the unit value are terminal. Hence every $F(\alpha_x)$ is an equivalence, so step 6 gives $F\in L$. The equality $E=L$ is an equality of full subcategories, not just of their cores.

Combine the equivalences $r:E\to W$, $E=L\to E_0$, and $E_0\to\operatorname{Fun}^{\mathrm{fp}}(C,D)$. The section $s$ of $r$ is an equivalence: $rs$ is the identity and $r$ is an equivalence. Its composite with the other two restriction maps is exactly unary restriction $W\to\operatorname{Fun}^{\mathrm{fp}}(C,D)$. This proves the assertion. Each Kan-extension comparison above is an equivalence of full functor infinity categories supplied by a trivial Kan fibration; it therefore retains every natural transformation and all higher simplices. The coherent pointwise equivalence criterion ensures the vertical comparisons used above are natural equivalences in these functor categories.
